Input type: legacy `.crash` report, single crash, symbolicated, complete (Binary Images table present and terminated).

## 1. What happened

Chartwright shut down immediately after it started up, at the moment it tried to load one of its own add-on components. macOS refused to run that component because its security seal did not match its contents, so the system killed the app.

## 2. The core issue

A code page of the bundled framework `NGPlotEngine` failed signature validation. `Termination Reason: CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` and `Exception Type: EXC_CRASH (SIGKILL (Code Signature Invalid))` mean the kernel terminated the process (SIGKILL — an immediate, uncatchable kill) rather than the app choosing to exit. Code signing seals a binary by storing a hash of every page; when a page is read into memory and its hash does not match the seal, macOS kills the process. The Application Specific Information block names the exact file — `/Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A/NGPlotEngine` — with `code signature invalid (errno=1)` and `codeBlobOffset=0x0041C000`. The most likely cause is that this framework binary was altered on disk after it was signed, or its signature was stripped/replaced without re-sealing.

Alternative reading: the file is intact but its pages cannot be validated because the app bundle was copied in a way that damaged the framework's `Versions/A` symlink structure or extended attributes — would be confirmed by running `codesign --verify --deep --strict /Applications/Chartwright.app` and checking whether it reports a modified resource versus a valid seal.

## 3. Why it happened

The signature check fires when `dyld` (the dynamic linker — the part of macOS that maps executable code into a running process) maps the framework's segments. Frame 3 of thread 0 shows `dyld4::APIs::dlopen_from`, so this framework was loaded on demand via `dlopen()` (a runtime call that loads a library after the app is already running), not linked at launch. `System Integrity Protection: enabled` is recorded, and on this Mac — `OS Version: macOS 15.5 (24F74)`, `Code Type: ARM-64 (Native)` — Apple silicon enforces valid code signatures for all executable pages with no opt-out. Anything that rewrites a signed binary invalidates the seal: post-signing modification, a corrupted or partial download, a build/CI step that touches the binary after `codesign` ran, or an installer that copies the bundle without preserving symlinks and metadata. The report gives no team identifier or entitlement fields, so a Team ID mismatch cannot be confirmed or ruled out from this evidence.

## 4. Why it crashed this way

No crash occurred inside the app's own logic. The backtrace is short and unambiguous: frame 5 is `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)`, frame 4 is `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()`, so the app had launched successfully and was in its startup callback when it asked for the plugin. Frames 3 through 0 are all in `dyld` — `dlopen_from`, `JustInTimeLoader::makeLaunchLoader`, `Loader::mapSegments`, and finally `SyscallDelegate::mapFileReadable`, which is where the file's pages are mapped into memory. Validation happens at that mapping step, so the failure surfaces in dyld rather than in Chartwright's code. `Exception Codes: 0x0000000000000000, 0x0000000000000000` carry no additional detail; the useful signal is entirely in the Termination Reason and the dyld message. `Exception Note: EXC_CORPSE_NOTIFY` simply means the kernel preserved the dead process so this report could be written. Because SIGKILL is delivered by the kernel, no exception handler or `dlopen` error path in the app could intercept it — hence a hard termination instead of a graceful "plugin failed to load" message. The distinction matters for diagnosis: this is a runtime failure at first-launch plugin load, not a missing-library failure, since dyld found the file and rejected its contents.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)

1. Verify the shipped bundle and identify what is unsealed:
   ```
   codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4 /Applications/Chartwright.app
   codesign -dvvv /Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/Chartwright.app
   ```
2. Confirm nothing modifies the framework binary after signing — strip, install_name_tool, `otool`-based patching, resource copying, or a post-build script running after the "Sign" phase in Xcode's Build Phases order.
3. Sign inside-out: sign each embedded framework first, then the outer app, and set "Other Code Signing Flags" so nested code is not re-signed after the outer seal:
   ```
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: ..." \
     Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: ..." Chartwright.app
   ```
4. Ship as a signed disk image or `pkg` and notarize it (notarization — Apple's automated scan that staples an approval ticket to the build), so the framework's symlinks and metadata survive distribution intact:
   ```
   xcrun notarytool submit Chartwright.dmg --keychain-profile "AC" --wait
   xcrun stapler staple Chartwright.dmg
   ```
5. Make `loadRenderer()` fail gracefully — check the `dlerror()` string and present a repair prompt — so a bad plugin never reaches an unrecoverable state at startup. Note this only improves reporting; SIGKILL from an invalid page cannot be caught.
6. Add a CI gate that runs `codesign --verify --deep --strict` on the final artifact before release, and validate on Apple silicon specifically, where signature enforcement is unconditional.

## 6. The fix (user-side)

1. Delete `/Applications/Chartwright.app`, empty the Trash, and re-download version 11.3.0 from the official source — a partial or interrupted download is the most common cause of this exact error.
2. If you installed by dragging the app out of a `.zip` or copying it between drives or servers, install from the developer's `.dmg` or installer package instead; copying can damage the internal file links this app relies on.
3. If any tool has touched the app — an "app cleaner," an optimizer, an antivirus quarantine/repair, or a plugin patch — remove that modification and reinstall a clean copy.
4. If a fresh reinstall still fails, send the developer this report and note the file named in it: `Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework`. Do not disable macOS security protections to work around it.

macOS Crash Report Analyzer v1.1

Input type: legacy `.crash` report (text format), single crash, symbolicated backtrace, report appears complete.

## 1. What happened

Chartwright quit immediately after starting up because macOS decided one of the app's own bundled components had been altered or damaged. The system refused to load it and shut the app down for safety.

## 2. The core issue

The app called `dlopen()` (a function that loads a code library while the program is already running) on its bundled framework at `/Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A/NGPlotEngine`, and dyld (the dynamic linker — the part of macOS that maps libraries into a running process) rejected it with `code signature invalid (errno=1)`. Termination Reason reads `CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page`, meaning the actual bytes on a memory page of that framework did not match what its code signature (a cryptographic seal recording the exact contents of each page at signing time) promised. The Application Specific Information block names the exact signature blob involved: `codeBlobOffset=0x0041C000, codeBlobSize=0x00009B40`. Because the mismatch is at page level rather than a missing or malformed signature, the file was signed at some point but its contents no longer match that seal. Alternative reading: the framework's signature is intact but is rejected by Library Validation because it is signed by a different Team ID than the main app — would be confirmed by checking `codesign -dvvv` on both binaries and the app's `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` entitlement.

## 3. Why it happened

The framework lives inside the app bundle (`Contents/Frameworks/`), so it is the developer's own code, not a system library. Its bytes diverged from its signature — the usual causes are modifying a binary after signing it (running `install_name_tool`, `strip`, or a bundling script post-signature), signing the outer app without re-signing the nested framework, or the file being corrupted or partially written during download, copy, or update. The `OS Version: macOS 15.5 (24F74)` field shows a current OS, and `Code Type: ARM-64 (Native)` on an Apple Silicon Mac means signature enforcement is unconditional — arm64 binaries must carry a valid signature, with no ad-hoc escape that Intel builds historically enjoyed. `System Integrity Protection: enabled` is the default state and is not itself the cause. Nothing in the report points to a missing library or an OS version mismatch; the file was found, it simply failed verification.

## 4. Why it crashed this way

Exception Type is `EXC_CRASH (SIGKILL (Code Signature Invalid))` — SIGKILL is an unblockable termination signal, so the process was killed outright by the kernel rather than being allowed to handle an error. Frame 5 of thread 0 is `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)`, which places the failure at launch time, in the app's startup callback, not during later use. Frame 4, `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()`, is the app's own code deliberately loading the plugin framework at runtime. Frames 3 through 0 walk into dyld: `dlopen_from` → `makeLaunchLoader` → `Loader::mapSegments` → `SyscallDelegate::mapFileReadable`, which is the moment dyld asks the kernel to map the framework's pages into memory. The kernel validates each page against the signature at that mapping step and returned `errno=1` (EPERM, "operation not permitted"), which is why the crash sits in the mapping helper rather than in the app. Because this happened inside `dlopen()` — a runtime load rather than a link-time dependency — the app got far enough to reach `main` (frame 7) and post `-[NSApplication _postDidFinishNotification]` (frame 6) before dying, which is why this presents as a crash a moment after the icon bounces rather than an instant nothing-happens failure. `Exception Codes: 0x0...0, 0x0...0` carry no additional address information, consistent with a policy kill rather than a memory fault.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)

1. Verify the shipped bundle to confirm the finding:
   ```
   codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4 /Applications/Chartwright.app
   codesign -vvv /Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   ```
2. Audit the build pipeline for any step that touches a binary *after* signing — `install_name_tool`, `strip`, `lipo`, resource injection, or a version-stamping script. Move every such step before the signing step.
3. Sign inside-out: nested frameworks first, then the outer app. Never rely on a single outer sign to cover already-signed nested code.
   ```
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: ..." \
     Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     --sign "Developer ID Application: ..." Chartwright.app
   ```
4. Confirm both binaries carry the same Team ID via `codesign -dvvv`. If the framework is legitimately from a third party with a different Team ID, either re-sign it under your identity or add `com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation` to the app's entitlements (Library Validation = the hardened runtime rule that only lets a process load code signed by the same team or Apple).
5. Use `ditto` rather than `cp` or a zip tool when packaging or copying the bundle, so extended attributes and signature metadata survive intact.
6. Notarize and staple the final artifact, then test from a fresh download on a clean machine — not the build machine, where a stale copy may mask the problem.

## 6. The fix (user-side)

1. Delete the app: drag `/Applications/Chartwright.app` to the Trash, then empty the Trash.
2. Download a fresh copy directly from Northgate's official site or the Mac App Store, and install it again — a truncated or interrupted download is a common cause of this exact failure.
3. If you use any antivirus, "app cleaner," or optimizer utility, exclude the Applications folder from it; these tools sometimes modify app files and invalidate their seal.
4. If the fresh copy still fails, send this crash report to the developer and note that the message reads `code signature invalid` for `NGPlotEngine.framework` — it is a packaging problem on their side, not something you can repair.

macOS Crash Report Analyzer v1.1

Input type: legacy crash report (`.crash`), single crash, symbolicated backtrace, report appears complete (Binary Images table and VM Region Summary both present).

## 1. What happened
The app started up, tried to load one of its own bundled add-on components, and macOS immediately shut the app down because that component's security seal did not match its contents. The app never got past its launch sequence.

## 2. The core issue
macOS refused to run `NGPlotEngine.framework` because its code signature (the cryptographic seal that proves a binary has not been altered since the developer signed it) failed validation. The Application Specific Information states plainly: `code signature invalid (errno=1)` for `/Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework/Versions/A/NGPlotEngine`. `Termination Reason: CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` means a specific memory page of that binary did not hash-match the values recorded in its signature, so the kernel killed the process rather than execute unverified code. The exception line confirms the mechanism: `EXC_CRASH (SIGKILL (Code Signature Invalid))` — SIGKILL is an unblockable termination signal sent by the system, not a fault inside the app's own logic. The most likely cause is that the framework binary was modified, replaced, or damaged after it was signed.

Alternative reading: the framework was signed with a different identity or was never re-signed after a post-build modification — would be confirmed by running `codesign -dvvv` on the framework and comparing its `TeamIdentifier` and `CDHash` against the outer app bundle.

## 3. Why it happened
The crash log shows the framework being opened at runtime via `dlopen` (frame 3, `dyld4::APIs::dlopen_from`) rather than being linked at launch, so its signature was validated only at that moment. On `Code Type: ARM-64 (Native)` — Apple Silicon — every executable page must carry a valid signature; there is no unsigned-code path, unlike older Intel Macs. The reported `sliceOffset=0x00000000, codeBlobOffset=0x0041C000, codeBlobSize=0x00009B40` indicates the signature blob was found and parsed, so this is a content mismatch, not a missing signature. `System Integrity Protection: enabled` confirms the platform's enforcement was fully active. Common origins of this exact state are a post-signing build step that rewrote the binary, a partial or corrupted install, or a third-party/updater process replacing the framework in place.

## 4. Why it crashed this way
This was a runtime crash during launch, not a link-time failure: `main` (thread 0, frame 7) had already run, AppKit had reached `-[NSApplication _postDidFinishNotification]` (frame 6), and the app's own `CWAppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching(_:)` (frame 5) called `NGPluginHost.loadRenderer()` (frame 4). That call entered `dlopen` (frame 3 — the function that loads a library on demand), which handed off to dyld (the dynamic linker, the part of macOS that maps libraries into memory). Frames 2 through 0 show dyld mapping the framework's segments: `JustInTimeLoader::makeLaunchLoader`, `Loader::mapSegments`, then `SyscallDelegate::mapFileReadable`, where the kernel verifies each page against the signature as it is mapped. The verification failed there, which is why `Termination Reason` names an *Invalid Page* rather than a missing or malformed signature. Because the kernel kills such a process outright, the app had no opportunity to catch an error or fall back to a no-plugin mode — `dlopen` never returned. `Exception Codes: 0x0000000000000000, 0x0000000000000000` carry no additional detail, consistent with a policy kill rather than a memory fault. Only three binaries appear in Binary Images (the app, dyld, AppKit), confirming `NGPlotEngine` was never successfully mapped.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)
1. Confirm the mismatch locally on the shipped bundle:
   ```
   codesign -vvv --strict /Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   codesign -dvvv /Applications/Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   ```
2. Audit the build for any step that touches the framework binary *after* signing — `strip`, `install_name_tool`, resource copying, or a custom Run Script phase. Move all of it before the signing step; any byte changed after signing produces exactly this `Invalid Page` result.
3. Re-sign inside-out (nested code first, app bundle last), using the same identity for both:
   ```
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     -s "Developer ID Application: ..." \
     Chartwright.app/Contents/Frameworks/NGPlotEngine.framework
   codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp \
     -s "Developer ID Application: ..." Chartwright.app
   ```
4. Verify Gatekeeper acceptance (Gatekeeper is macOS's policy check on downloaded software) before shipping: `spctl -a -vvv -t exec Chartwright.app`.
5. Notarize and staple the ticket (notarization is Apple's automated malware scan of a signed build), then re-verify the whole bundle after stapling.
6. Ship via a signed DMG or `.pkg` rather than a loose folder or an updater that overwrites `Contents/Frameworks` in place, since in-place replacement is a frequent source of this failure on installed copies.

## 6. The fix (user-side)
1. Drag `/Applications/Chartwright.app` to the Trash and empty it — a partially damaged copy cannot be repaired in place.
2. Re-download Chartwright 11.3.0 from the vendor's official site or the Mac App Store and install the fresh copy.
3. If you installed any Chartwright plugins, add-ons, or third-party patches, do not reinstall them yet; test the clean app first, since an add-on replacing `NGPlotEngine` would cause exactly this.
4. If it still quits on launch, send this crash report to Northgate support and mention `CODESIGNING 2 Invalid Page` — the signed build itself may be at fault, which only they can correct.

macOS Crash Report Analyzer v1.1

Input type: legacy `.crash` report, single crash, unsymbolicated (frames show raw addresses with `???` and `0 + offset` instead of symbol names), and incomplete — only thread 3 is listed and the usual trailing summary sections after `Binary Images` are absent.

## 1. What happened

LedgerSync was running normally and then quit unexpectedly when one of its background tasks tried to use something that wasn't there. This was a runtime failure, not a startup or installation problem.

## 2. The core issue

The app dereferenced a null pointer — `Exception Type: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)` (a memory-access violation: the process touched memory it is not allowed to touch) with `Exception Codes: KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000010`. Address `0x10` is 16 bytes past address zero, the classic signature of reading a field or calling through a member of an object that was never initialized or was already released. The register dump backs this up: `rax: 0x0000000000000000` (a null value) and `rcx: 0x0000000000000010` (that value plus a 16-byte field offset). The faulting thread is `Crashed Thread: 3`, and frames 2 and 3 are inside LedgerSync's own image (`0x10a2f4118` and `0x10a301b90`, both within the `0x10a2c0000 - 0x10a44bfff` range listed in Binary Images), so app code is on the stack when it happens. Frames 0 and 1 (`0x00007ff8091a4c50`, `0x00007ff8091b1a34`) fall outside every range in the Binary Images table, so the immediate caller cannot be attributed to any named library from this report.

*Alternative reading:* memory corruption or a use-after-free rather than a plain uninitialized pointer — frame 6 is `0x0000000000000000`, and a zeroed return address at the base of the stack can indicate a damaged frame chain; this would be confirmed by running the same workload under Address Sanitizer or Zombie Objects and by a symbolicated trace for frames 0–1.

## 3. Why it happened

`Code Type: X86-64 (Translated)` means this is an Intel (x86-64) build running under Rosetta 2 (Apple's translation layer that runs Intel binaries on Apple Silicon Macs), so the app ships no native arm64 slice for this machine. The crash is on thread 3 while frames 4 and 5 sit in `libsystem_kernel.dylib` and `libsystem_pthread.dylib`, i.e. a worker thread the app spawned itself, which is where uninitialized-state and race-condition bugs typically surface. Beyond that, the report does not name the function or object involved, because the backtrace carries no symbols. The OS is `macOS 14.5 (23F79)` and there is no `Termination Reason` pointing at dyld (the dynamic linker, which loads shared libraries at launch), code signing, or a sandbox denial — `Termination Reason: NAMESPACE SIGNAL, CODE 11` is simply the segmentation-fault signal restated. So nothing here indicates a missing framework, an entitlement problem, or a Gatekeeper/notarization issue.

## 4. Why it crashed this way

No termination came from the OS policy layer; the process killed itself with a hardware memory fault. The kernel reported `KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000010`, meaning nothing is mapped at that address and never will be — page zero is deliberately left unmapped so that null dereferences fail immediately and loudly rather than corrupting data. Because `rip: 0x00007ff8091a4c50` matches frame 0, the fault happened at the instruction currently executing in an unattributed image, not in LedgerSync's own code directly. LedgerSync's frames 2 and 3 are the callers, so the app handed a bad or null value into that code rather than crashing on its own instruction. This was a runtime crash, not a launch crash: the app had reached the point of creating and running secondary threads, and thread 3 was executing app logic when it failed. The presence of `libsystem_pthread.dylib` at frame 5 confirms thread 3 is a pthread the app started. Frame 6 reading `0x0000000000000000` is not a real frame; it is the null terminator at the base of a thread stack or a sign the unwinder lost the chain. Because the whole backtrace is unsymbolicated, the specific function, class, and line cannot be named from this report alone.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)

1. Symbolicate before anything else. Find the `.dSYM` (debug symbol bundle produced alongside a release build) whose UUID matches `A7819243-A4B5-46D7-E8F9-A0B1C2D3E4F5` and resolve the app frames:
   ```
   atos -o LedgerSync.app.dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/LedgerSync \
        -arch x86_64 -l 0x10a2c0000 0x10a2f4118 0x10a301b90
   ```
2. Once frames 2 and 3 are named, audit that code path for a pointer or object reference used before assignment or after release — the `0x10` offset says a member was read off a null base.
3. Because the crash is on a spawned pthread (thread 3), check that any shared state it touches is created before the thread starts and guarded (`NSLock`, a serial `DispatchQueue`, or `@synchronized`); a torn-down-while-in-use object produces exactly this fault.
4. Reproduce under Xcode's diagnostics: enable **Address Sanitizer**, **Zombie Objects**, and **Thread Sanitizer** in the scheme's Run > Diagnostics tab, then exercise the same background workload.
5. Ship a universal binary so this stops running under translation — set `ARCHS = arm64 x86_64` (Build Settings > Architectures), rebuild, and verify with `lipo -archs /Applications/LedgerSync.app/Contents/MacOS/LedgerSync`.
6. Add a defensive early return or assertion at the entry to that thread's work function so a null dependency logs a diagnostic instead of faulting.

## 6. The fix (user-side)

1. Quit and relaunch LedgerSync — this was a runtime fault, not an install problem, so a restart will usually get you working again.
2. Note what you were doing right before the crash (which sync, which file, which window) and send that to the developer with this crash report; it is the fastest route to a fix.
3. Check for an app update: **LedgerSync menu > Check for Updates**, or the App Store's Updates tab. Version `2.0.4 (2040)` is what crashed, and a newer build may already address it.
4. Ask the developer for an Apple Silicon (arm64) build — your copy is the Intel version running through Rosetta translation, and a native build will also run faster.

macOS Crash Report Analyzer v1.1

Input type: legacy `.crash` text crash report, single crash, unsymbolicated — frames show raw addresses and `???` with no symbol names, so per-frame attribution is limited.

## 1. What happened
The app was running normally and then quit suddenly while doing background work. One of its background tasks tried to use a piece of memory that wasn't there, and macOS shut the app down.

## 2. The core issue
The crash is a memory access fault: `Exception Type: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)` (EXC_BAD_ACCESS — the app touched an address the memory system refused; SIGSEGV — the Unix "segmentation fault" signal for exactly that). `Exception Codes: KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000010` points at address 16, and the register dump backs it up: `rax: 0x0000000000000000` with `rcx: 0x0000000000000010` — the classic shape of reading a field 16 bytes into an object pointer that was null. Frames 2 and 3 of the crashed thread sit inside `LedgerSync` itself (`0x000000010a2f4118` and `0x000000010a301b90`, both within the app's image range `0x10a2c0000 - 0x10a44bfff` from Binary Images), so the bad pointer originates in the app's own code, not in a system framework. Alternative reading: a use-after-free, where the object was valid earlier and freed by another thread — would be confirmed by running with Zombie Objects or MallocStackLogging enabled and seeing a freed-object message instead of a null read.

## 3. Why it happened
The report shows no missing library, no code-signing or entitlement failure, and no launch-time abort — `Termination Reason: NAMESPACE SIGNAL, CODE 11` is just the segmentation signal, so this is an ordinary in-app pointer bug rather than an environment problem. `Code Type: X86-64 (Translated)` means an Intel-only build is running under Rosetta 2 (Apple's translation layer that runs x86-64 code on Apple Silicon Macs), so the machine is Apple Silicon and the app ships no native `arm64` slice. Nothing in the report attributes the fault to translation itself; it is recorded here as context, not as the cause. `OS Version: macOS 14.5 (23F79)` shows a current, supported system, so this is not an OS feature-gating mismatch. The exact API that returned or held the null value cannot be named because frames 0 and 1 are `???` at `0x00007ff8091a4c50` and `0x00007ff8091b1a34`, addresses that fall outside every range listed in Binary Images.

## 4. Why it crashed this way
This was a runtime crash, not a launch failure: the faulting thread is `Crashed Thread: 3`, a worker thread, and frame 5 is `libsystem_pthread.dylib` (the system library that implements threads), meaning the app had been running long enough to spawn and use background threads. The stack reads outward from the fault at frame 0 through two unresolved system frames, into the app's own code at frames 2 and 3, then down into `libsystem_kernel.dylib` and `libsystem_pthread.dylib` — the app called into system code, which then dereferenced the bad pointer. Because the target address `0x10` lies in the first page of memory, which macOS deliberately leaves unmapped to catch null pointer bugs, the hardware trapped immediately and the kernel delivered SIGSEGV rather than letting corrupted data spread. Frame 6 shows `0x0000000000000000`, an address of zero — the stack walk hit a null return address and stopped, which is consistent with a damaged or simply exhausted frame chain at the thread's root. The unresolved frames 0 and 1 are the reason no specific system API can be blamed: their addresses are not covered by any entry in the Binary Images table, so the crash reporter had nothing to resolve them against. Everything actionable therefore rests on frames 2 and 3, both inside `LedgerSync` at offsets `+213272` and `+269200` from the load address `0x10a2c0000`.

## 5. The fix (developer-side)
1. Symbolicate the two app frames first (symbolication — mapping addresses back to source lines using the debug-symbol bundle produced at build time). Locate the `.dSYM` matching UUID `A7819243-A4B5-46D7-E8F9-A0B1C2D3E4F5` and run:
   ```
   atos -o LedgerSync.app.dSYM/Contents/Resources/DWARF/LedgerSync \
        -arch x86_64 -l 0x10a2c0000 0x10a2f4118 0x10a301b90
   ```
2. Inspect the two resolved call sites for a pointer or object reference used without a nil/null check before being passed into a system call.
3. Reproduce under the Address Sanitizer and with Zombie Objects enabled (Product > Scheme > Edit Scheme > Diagnostics) to separate a plain null from a use-after-free.
4. Since the fault is on a secondary thread, audit shared state reachable from that code path with the Thread Sanitizer; a pointer nulled or freed by another thread mid-use fits the evidence.
5. Ship a universal binary — `Code Type: X86-64 (Translated)` shows this build has no `arm64` slice; set `ARCHS = $(ARCHS_STANDARD)`, rebuild, and confirm with `lipo -archs /Applications/LedgerSync.app/Contents/MacOS/LedgerSync`.
6. Add a crash-reporting hook that captures the same thread's symbolicated stack in the field, so future reports arrive with frames 0 and 1 resolved.

## 6. The fix (user-side)
1. Reopen the app and note what you were doing when it quit — background sync or export activity is the likely trigger, since the crash was on a background task.
2. Check for an update: the app's own menu, the App Store, or the developer's site — version `2.0.4 (2040)` is what crashed.
3. Ask the developer whether a native Apple Silicon build is available; your Mac is currently running this app through Rosetta 2 translation.
4. Send the developer this crash report along with the steps that led to it; the fault is inside the app's code and only they can correct it.

## 1. What happened

The app was running normally and then quit unexpectedly while doing work in the background. One of its background tasks tried to read data from a memory location that held nothing, and macOS shut the app down on the spot.

## 2. The core issue

`Exception Type: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)` with `Exception Codes: KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000010` means the process touched memory it does not own (EXC_BAD_ACCESS is the Mach exception for an invalid memory access; SIGSEGV is the matching Unix "segmentation fault" signal). The address `0x10` is 16 bytes past zero — the classic signature of reading a field off a pointer that was null rather than a real object. ## 1. What happened
Loomstack quit about half a second after the user chose "Import Folder." The imported folder's assets referred to each other in a loop, and the app kept following that loop until it ran out of working space and was killed.

## 2. The core issue
Thread 6 (`com.loomstack.sync`) ran away in unbounded recursion: the Application Specific Information reports `Recursion depth at fault: 8188 frames in LSGraphResolver.resolve(_:visited:)`, and frames 0–4 of the crashed thread all sit at the same address `0x000000010b2f4118` for that function. The input contained a loop — `cycle detected in dependency graph: node "asset:root" -> "asset:layer-04" -> "asset:mask-11" -> "asset:layer-04"` — so `resolve(_:visited:)` never reached a base case. That exhausted the thread's 512 KB stack (`stack size 524288 bytes`) and touched the guard page (a deliberately unwritable memory page placed just past a thread's stack so overflow faults instead of corrupting other memory): `Thread 6 stack guard page hit at 0x00007ff7b0e41ff8`. ## 3. Why it happened
Two preference flags put the app on an unguarded code path: `com.loomstack.desktop.experimentalGraphResolver = 1` and `com.loomstack.desktop.maxRecursionGuard = 0`, with the console line `warning: experimental resolver enabled; recursion guard disabled`. The resolver also declined to repair the input it had already diagnosed: `error: dependency cycle will not be broken automatically`. The process is running under Rosetta (Apple's translation layer that runs Intel x86-64 code on Apple Silicon Macs) — `Code Type: X86-64 (Translated)` and `Rosetta: translated binary executing on arm64e host` — and the report itself flags the consequence: `warning: running under Rosetta; stack limits differ from arm64`. Translated frames are generally larger, so a given recursion depth consumes stack faster than it would in a native build. The trigger was user input: `last user action "Import Folder" 412ms before fault`, matching frame 5 `LSAssetImporter.importFolder(at:)`.

## 4. Why it crashed this way
This was a runtime crash on a background worker, not a launch failure — frames 7 and 8 show `_dispatch_call_block_and_release` and `_pthread_wqthread`, so the work ran on a Grand Central Dispatch queue thread rather than the main thread. `Exception Type: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGBUS)` with `KERN_PROTECTION_FAILURE at 0x00007ff7b0e41ff8` is the signature of writing to memory the process is not permitted to write, which here is the guard page named at that exact same address. Stack overflow surfaces as a protection failure rather than a clean "out of stack" error because the CPU simply sees a store into a protected page. `Termination Reason: NAMESPACE SIGNAL, CODE 10` is signal 10, SIGBUS, confirming the same event from the kernel's side.

The backtrace is deliberately shallow: the reporter collapsed 8188 identical frames into five repeats of `LSGraphResolver.resolve(_:visited:) + 296`, all at one address, which is what pure self-recursion looks like.    func resolve(_ node: Node, visited: inout Set<NodeID>) throws {
       guard visited.insert(node.id).inserted else {
           throw ResolveError.cycle(at: node.id)   // e.g. "asset:layer-04"

## 1. What happened

Loomstack quit while importing a folder because a piece of its file-organizing logic chased its own tail and never stopped. It ran out of working memory space for that task and the system shut the app down.

## 2. The core issue

Thread 6 (`com.loomstack.sync`) overflowed its stack (the fixed-size scratch memory a thread uses for nested function calls). Frames 0–4 all sit at the same address, `0x000000010b2f4118` in `LSGraphResolver.resolve(_:visited:)`, and the annotation reports `Recursion depth at fault: 8188 frames` in that function. The function called itself indefinitely because `LSGraphResolver: cycle detected in dependency graph` shows the graph loops: `"asset:root" -> "asset:layer-04" -> "asset:mask-11" -> "asset:layer-04"`. The `visited:` parameter implies a cycle-tracking set that was not preventing re-entry. The annotation `Thread 6 stack guard page hit at 0x00007ff7b0e41ff8; stack size 524288 bytes` confirms the thread ran past the end of its 512 KB stack into the guard page (a deliberately unwritable memory page placed at the stack's end to catch overflow).

## 3. Why it happened

Two preference values in the report explain why nothing stopped the recursion: `com.loomstack.desktop.experimentalGraphResolver = 1` and `com.loomstack.desktop.maxRecursionGuard = 0`, matched by the console line `"warning: experimental resolver enabled; recursion guard disabled"`. With the guard set to zero there was no depth ceiling to abort the descent. The console also records `"error: dependency cycle will not be broken automatically"`, so the resolver detected the loop but had no policy to break it. The trigger was user-initiated: `LSTelemetry: last user action "Import Folder" 412ms before fault`, matching frame 5 `LSAssetImporter.importFolder(at:)` and frame 6 `-[LSDocument beginImport:]`. Execution environment is a contributing factor — `Code Type: X86-64 (Translated)` and `Rosetta: translated binary executing on arm64e host` mean this Intel-built app runs through Rosetta (Apple's x86-64 translation layer on Apple Silicon), and the console notes `"warning: running under Rosetta; stack limits differ from arm64"`. The work ran on a dispatch queue worker thread (frames 7–8, `_dispatch_call_block_and_release` and `_pthread_wqthread`), which gets a much smaller stack than the main thread — here 524288 bytes.

## 4. Why it crashed this way

- The exception is `EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGBUS)` with `KERN_PROTECTION_FAILURE at 0x00007ff7b0e41ff8` — a memory access the hardware permitted no write to, rather than an unmapped address. That is the signature of hitting a guard page, not of a null-pointer dereference.
- The second exception code line, `0x0000000000000002, 0x00007ff7b0e41ff8`, marks the access as a write to that exact address, and the same address appears in `Thread 6 stack guard page hit at 0x00007ff7b0e41ff8`. The write was the next stack frame's prologue pushing past the limit.
- `Termination Reason: NAMESPACE SIGNAL, CODE 10` is signal 10, SIGBUS — the kernel killed the process on the fatal memory-access signal rather than on an internal `abort()`.
- This is a runtime crash, not a launch crash: the app reached version-specific code (`Version: 6.1.3 (6130)`), loaded 412 images per the dyld annotation, and had already processed a user action 412 ms earlier.
- `Triggered by Thread: 6` and `Crashed Thread: 6 com.loomstack.sync` place blame on the background sync thread, not the main thread, so the UI was likely still responsive up to the moment of death.
- Only frames 0–4 of the recursion appear in the backtrace; the crash reporter elides the repetition, and the annotation supplies the real count of 8188.
- Because the stack was exhausted, no Swift runtime trap or error message could be produced — there was no room left to run a handler. That is why you see a hardware fault instead of a clean assertion.
- `LSSyncCoordinator: 3 pending merges abandoned` indicates in-flight work was lost at the fault, so this crash carries a data-consistency risk beyond the quit itself.
- The dyld line `loaded 412 images, 3 with mismatched platform` is consistent with Rosetta translation and is not implicated in the faulting frames (dyld = the dynamic linker, the part of macOS that loads shared libraries).

## 5. The fix (developer-side)

1. Make the `visited:` set actually terminate the walk — insert each node before descending and return immediately on a hit:

   ```swift
   func resolve(_ node: Node, visited: inout Set<NodeID>) throws {
       guard visited.insert(node.id).inserted else {
           throw ResolveError.cycle(node.id)   // "asset:layer-04" case
       }
       for dep in node.dependencies { try resolve(dep, visited: &visited) }
   }
   ```

2. Stop shipping a zero depth ceiling. Treat `maxRecursionGuard = 0` as "unset" and fall back to a sane default rather than "unlimited":

   ```swift
   let guardDepth = max(defaults.integer(forKey: "maxRecursionGuard"), 512)
   ```

3. Convert the resolver to an explicit iterative worklist (an array-backed stack plus a colour/`inProgress` map) so depth is bounded by heap, not by the 524288-byte thread stack.
4. Give the import work a larger stack instead of a dispatch queue worker: create a dedicated `Thread` and set `thread.stackSize = 8 << 20` before `start()`.
5. Ship a native `arm64` slice so the app stops running under Rosetta — build a universal binary and confirm with `lipo -archs /Applications/Loomstack.app/Contents/MacOS/Loomstack`; then re-test the import on Apple Silicon, since the console flags `"stack limits differ from arm64"`.
6. Gate `experimentalGraphResolver` behind an internal-only flag, and surface the already-detected cycle (`"error: dependency cycle will not be broken automatically"`) to the user as a recoverable error instead of continuing to descend.

2. Avoid re-running "Import Folder" on the same folder until then — that action, 412 ms before the crash, is what triggered it.
